title: Business: exam writing
course: Pearson BTEC Level 3 National Business · Unit 2 set task practice (Technective)
note: The questions, structures and mark schemes are written for this site. The writing structures are a standard approach until your teacher's structure is added. The site doesn't copy the Technective booklet: use your own copy for the facts and figures.

explain.name: Explain

steps.label: Point
steps.hint: Name one clear idea, e.g. a characteristic, advantage or effect.

steps.label: Explain
steps.hint: Say why or how, with a link word: because… so… which means…

steps.label: Use the case
steps.hint: Back it up with a fact or number from the case study.

explain.tip: One point, fully developed and applied, beats three listed points.

calculate.name: Calculate and explain

steps.label: Formula
steps.hint: Write the formula you are using.

steps.label: Working
steps.hint: Show each step with the numbers from the case, and the units (£, %).

steps.label: Meaning
steps.hint: Say what the answer shows about the business.

calculate.tip: Always show working: you can get marks for method even if the final answer is wrong.

analyse.name: Analyse

steps.label: Point
steps.hint: Make a clear point that answers the question.

steps.label: Chain of reasoning
steps.hint: Build connected steps: this leads to… which means… as a result…

steps.label: Use the case
steps.hint: Use specific evidence from the case: names, numbers, facts.

steps.label: Impact
steps.hint: Finish with the effect on the business, e.g. on sales, costs, profit or reputation.

analyse.tip: Aim for two well-developed points, each with a chain of reasoning, rather than lots of short ones. No conclusion is needed.

evaluate.name: Assess / Evaluate

steps.label: Argument for
steps.hint: Point, chain of reasoning and evidence from the case on one side.

steps.label: Argument against
steps.hint: Point, chain of reasoning and evidence from the case on the other side.

steps.label: Judgement
steps.hint: Answer the question directly: which matters most, or what should they do, and why?

steps.label: It depends on…
steps.hint: Name the key factor that could change your judgement.

evaluate.tip: Both sides need evidence from the case, and your judgement must follow from your arguments. A judgement with no reason gets few marks.

cases.name: Technective
cases.text: Use your own Technective pre-release booklet for this case: the set task brief, the UK smartwatch market, the competitor profiles, the primary research report and the media options. This site doesn't copy the booklet, so have it open next to you and quote its facts and figures in your answers.

questions.q: Explain one reason why the UK smartwatch market is an opportunity for Technective.
pts: Identifies a reason, e.g. a large or growing number of users / demand from younger people / smaller brands gaining share / demand for affordable, differentiated watches
Explains why it is an opportunity, e.g. more potential customers, so Technective could gain sales and market share
Uses evidence from the booklet, e.g. a market-size, forecast or trend figure
questions.tip: Quote one specific figure or fact from the market section to support your point.

questions.q: Using the primary research, calculate the percentage of smartwatch owners who bought their watch to monitor health and fitness. Explain what your answer shows.
pts: Correct method: number who chose health and fitness ÷ number of smartwatch owners (not the whole sample) × 100
Accurate working with the booklet's figures, giving the answer as a percentage (1 decimal place)
Meaning, e.g. it is the most common reason, so a health and fitness focus could appeal to the largest group of buyers
questions.tip: Divide by the number of OWNERS, not the whole sample: only owners answered this question.

questions.q: Analyse how reliable Technective's primary research is for planning the campaign.
pts: Sample size is small compared with the number of UK smartwatch users, so it may not represent the whole market
Carried out in one location (a city shopping centre), so it may not reflect buyers elsewhere in the UK
The sample's age and gender profile doesn't match the market's main buyers, so results may be biased
Only over-16s were asked, which misses younger buyers, a growing group
It is recent, so it reflects current opinions in a fast-changing market
Impact: decisions on segment, price and features based on it carry some risk, so it should be checked against the secondary research
questions.tip: For each reliability point, say what it could lead to: wrong decisions about the segment, price or media.

questions.q: Analyse the threats that competitors pose to Technective's new smartwatch.
pts: Large brands hold big market shares and strong brand loyalty, so it is hard to win their customers
Low-cost brands and price wars push prices down, reducing Technective's possible profit margins
Competitors are launching affordable models aimed at general consumers, competing for the same buyers
Competitors use strong digital marketing, partnerships and sponsorship, raising the cost of being noticed
Competitor weaknesses, e.g. complaints about faults or data accuracy, show what Technective must avoid or can exploit
Impact on Technective: it needs a clear USP, a competitive price and targeted media to stand out
questions.tip: Name specific competitors from the booklet and link each threat to its effect on Technective.

questions.q: Explain one SMART objective Technective could set for the campaign.
pts: States a specific, measurable objective, e.g. a sales, awareness or social-media target with a number
Time-bound within the campaign's timescale, and achievable within the budget
Explains why it suits the campaign, linked to the chosen segment or research evidence
questions.tip: Check every letter of SMART is covered, and link the target to evidence from the booklet.

questions.q: Evaluate whether Technective should target health and fitness enthusiasts or technology enthusiasts.
pts: Health and fitness: the most common reason for buying, and fitness monitoring is the most expected feature
Health and fitness: specialist media (fitness magazines, sponsorship, influencers) reach this segment directly
Health and fitness: crowded with established competitors focused on fitness, so it is hard to stand out
Technology: the brand already sells phones and computers, so it can link the watch with its own products
Technology: buyers expect connectivity features (calls, messaging, payments), which fit Technective's expertise
Technology: trends show some buyers are bored of seeing the same features, so innovation would be needed
Judgement: a clear choice, supported by the research figures
It depends on, e.g. the price the segment will pay, or how well the features can be adapted
questions.tip: Use figures from the primary research for BOTH segments, then make a clear choice with an 'it depends on'.

questions.q: Justify a media plan for the campaign that stays within the budget and timescale in the brief.
pts: Chooses media that reach the chosen segment, using audience data from the media options
Uses a mix of media, e.g. digital (social ads, influencers) and traditional (magazines, posters, sponsorship)
Shows costs and totals that stay within the budget, spread across the timescale
Compares cost with reach, e.g. cost per reader or per click, to justify value for money
Rejects or limits expensive options with reasons, e.g. TV costs a large share of the budget
Links media to the campaign objectives and to competitor activity
Judgement on why this mix is the best use of the budget
It depends on, e.g. how results are monitored and the budget moved to what works
questions.tip: Use the budget planner below to check your totals, then justify each choice with audience data AND cost.

questions.q: Assess how external influences could affect Technective's campaign.
pts: Economic: the cost-of-living crisis makes buyers more price-sensitive, affecting price and message
Legal: data-protection and privacy rules affect health-data features and how they are promoted
Technological: fast change and lack of new features affect what the watch must offer
Social: trends towards style, customisation and fashion affect the product and media choice
Competitive pressure and price wars affect positioning
Judgement on which influence matters most for the campaign, and why
questions.tip: Use PESTLE headings to organise, but only discuss influences the booklet gives evidence for.

terms.d: Objectives that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound
A broad, long-term goal that a business wants to achieve
A specific, measurable target that helps a business achieve its aim
A planned set of marketing activities, over a set time, to achieve specific objectives
The specific group of customers a business aims its product and marketing at
Dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs or characteristics
Grouping customers by factors such as age, gender, income or occupation
Grouping customers by their lifestyle, values, interests and attitudes
Grouping customers by where they live, e.g. region, country, town or city
The total number of customers, or the total value of sales, in a market
The percentage of total sales in a market made by one business or brand
How a market is made up, e.g. how many businesses compete in it and how big they are
When a market has so many similar products that there is little room left for growth
The general direction a market is moving in over time, e.g. growing demand for a feature
New information collected first-hand by a business for its own purpose, e.g. a questionnaire
Information that already exists because someone else collected it, e.g. reports and statistics
Numerical information that can be counted and analysed, e.g. percentages
Information about opinions, feelings and reasons, usually given in words
The number of people who take part in a piece of research
How far research results can be trusted to be accurate and to give the same results again
A feature that makes a product different from, and better than, its competitors' products
Something that lets a business do better than its rivals, e.g. lower costs or a stronger brand
When customers keep buying from the same brand instead of switching to competitors
Another business selling similar products to the same customers
The combination of product, price, place and promotion used to market a product
Setting a high price to reflect high quality, status or exclusivity
Setting a low price at launch to attract customers and win market share quickly
Cutting prices for a short time, e.g. discounts or offers, to boost sales
When competitors keep cutting their prices to win customers from each other
Encouraging customers to buy a more expensive version or extra products
The full range of products that a business sells
A review of a business's internal strengths and weaknesses, and external opportunities and threats
A review of the political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors outside a business
A factor outside the business's control that affects it, e.g. the economy or new laws
Paying to support an event, team or person in return for promoting the brand
Working with people who have large social media followings to promote a product
Paying for an online advert each time someone clicks on it
The number of people who pass or visit a particular place, e.g. a shop or billboard
The channels used to send a marketing message, e.g. TV, social media, magazines or billboards
The amount of money set aside to spend on a marketing campaign
